THE CANADIAN ECONOMY
subsubtopic: PROPOSALS FOR IMPROVING ECONOMIC SITUATION-MOTION UNDER S.O. 43
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in light of the fact that unemployment is now 878,000, a record for the month of July, in light of the fact that second quarter job vacancies have dropped to only four per thousand from 14 per thousand three years ago, and in light of the fact that the bill for unemployment insurance benefits in May was $12 million per day, 1 move, seconded by the hon. member for St. John's East (Mr. McGrath):
That this House urges the government to adopt the following Progressive Conservative program for the economic reconstruction of this country: income tax cuts of $250 million to low and middle income earners; a cut in the federal sales tax on building materials to stimulate housing and create employment in the construction industry; long term Fiscal or tax contracts for companies investing in Atlantic Canada or Quebec; a new budget with major emphasis on private sector job creation; and a reallocation of government funds presently budgeted for inessential projects to direct job creation programs.

In accordance with the provisions of the resolution adopted by the House on Monday, July 25, 1977, having been satisfied after consultation with the Government, that the public interest requires that the House should meet at an earlier time during the adjournment, I hereby give notice that the House of Commons shall meet on Tuesday, August 9, 1977, at 2.00 o'clock p.m., for the

James Jerome Speaker
House of Commons Canada

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under Standing Order 43. As it is now clear an international cartel in uranium succeeded in rigging world prices, so that the floor price per pound of uranium was set in the $14 per pound range in the early part of 1974, and as it is now evident from the director's minutes of Ontario Hydro that this "world price" was proposed by Rio Algom in their uranium offer to Ontario Hydro of February 25, 1974, and that Denison in the same period proposed to Ontario Hydro a floor price of $14.50 per pound, I move, seconded by the hon. member for Don Valley (Mr. Gillies):
That a reference be made to the public accounts standing committee of this House so that the activities of this uranium cartel may be reviewed with particular reference to their impact on Canadian domestic consumers.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise on a matter of urgent and pressing necessity under the provisions of Standing Order 43. In the years since the current finance minister first joined the cabinet, he has been responsible first for the uranium cartel, for our present legacy of energy rises as minister of energy, and now, as Minister of Finance, for record inflation followed by record unemployment. speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I rise under the provisions of Standing Order 43 to move a motion which would permit us to accomplish what we came here to do. Since our convening at this time in emergency session has been prompted by a crisis in the country, the Canadian public expects us to debate the matter as soon as possible.
The ordinary rules of this House are such that many hours can be used discussing a number of other matters, thus deny-

ing us the possibility of getting to the debate at hand for some time and therefore at great additional cost to the Canadian taxpayers. I therefore move, seconded by the hon. member for Saint-Jacques (Mr. Guilbault):
That this House agrees to set aside all routine proceedings, including oral questions, and proceed with the emergency debate forthwith.
Furthermore, in order to preserve the prerogatives of members who wish to do so, that when all stages of the emergency legislation are passed, an additional sitting day be made available for the purpose of discussing matters that would normally be dealt with in routine proceedings.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, my question is for the Prime Minister and it comes in light of the fact that today's unemployment figures for the month of July are the highest in the history of Statistics Canada. Since it is very clear from the statistics revealed today that the job creating part of the budget of this spring simply has not taken hold, has not created the jobs that Canadians require, will the Prime Minister tell the House whether it is his intention to bring in a new budget at the earliest possible time, a budget that will include effective incentives to the Canadian private sector that will create the jobs that Canadians need?

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, while sharing the concern of the Leader of the Opposition on the high rate of unemployment, I would not agree with his feeling that the budget has not begun to take effect. If the hon. member looks at the figures for the first six months of the year, he will see that there has been a relatively strong increase in employment. Of course, the number of people entering the labour force has also been very high, and this is the cause of the present statistic. As to the solution, I will keep the hon. member's suggestion in mind.

At that time the President of the Treasury Board indicated that the government might have to move away from encouragement of the private sector and move toward direct public sector job creation.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. P. E. Trudeau (Prime Minister):
subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: OFFICIAL RESIDENCE OF PRIME MINISTER
speechtext:
Since the beginning of the current session, many questions related to the Prime Minister's official residences have been placed on the Order Paper. It seems therefore appropriate to place at this time on the official record of the House of Commons some notes on measures taken by successive Parliaments to provide official residences to the holder of the office of Prime Minister of Canada. The decision of the Government of Canada to make arrangements for an official residence for Canada's Prime Minister goes back to 1949, when it was announced in the House of Commons on September 30, by the Right Hon. C. D. Howe, Minister of Trade and Commerce. In his statement, Mr. Howe, after mentioning that Canada was one of the few countries that did not have an official residence for its Prime Minister, referred to "the difficulty of a Prime Minister, coming to Ottawa for an uncertain tenure, in obtaining the type of house suitable to the high office he holds". The Government had therefore decided to ask Parliament to make it possible to renovate the Edwards property (now known as 24 Sussex Drive) by making provision for the cost of alterations, repairs and future maintenance, and that if there was no serious opposition to this program, the House would be asked, in the estimates for 1950, to provide the necessary funds for that purpose. Mr. George A. Drew, Leader of the Opposition, supported the Government's decision in the following terms: ". .. I feel sure the decision is one which will meet with the general approval of the members of this house and of citizens in every part of Canada. Members of parliament know-it may not be known generally throughout the rest of the country-the extent to which the Prime Minister of Canada is called upon to receive official visitors. Certain duties which are essential to that high office should be a part of the responsibility of the state. I am not in a position to give any opinion as to the particular residence mentioned. I wish to express our satisfaction that the Prime Minister will have the opportunity of carrying on his official duties and receiving official visitors
Order Paper Questions
in a manner more in keeping with Canada's present position in world affairs. .. It will assist the Prime Minister of Canada, not only in receiving those important visitors but in carrying out his own heavy personal duties, to have a permanent home, where, as the elected head of the government of Canada, he can discharge his reponsibilities in a manner that will be in keeping with the status of Canada in the world today".
The Parliamentary Leaders of both the Cooperative Commonwealth Federation and the Social Credit Party also expressed concurrence with the proposal. Mr. M. J. Coldwell said that he was glad that the Prime Minister was to be suitably housed, while Mr. Solon E. Low, after welcoming the announcement, added that the Government .. should consider also the question of furnishing adequate recompense for him by way of indemnity. The prime ministers of this country have been notoriously underpaid. Over the years they have been called upon to make sacrifices far beyond the measure of the services they have given to the country". It should be noted that prior to the announcement, a number of MP's among them the Member for Fort William, the Rev. Daniel Mclvor, had suggested such a measure during the Address Debate. The following year, on June 7, 1950, the Government introduced the necessary legislation-"The Prime Minister's Residence Act"-which was passed the following day. The cost of renovation of the property, whether it might not have been more advisable to erect a new building, and other related matters, gave rise to debate. However, all parties supported the principle of the Bill. The consensus of the House can best be summarized by the following remarks of Mr. Coldwell. ".. . I think our country is doing the proper thing in conformity with what other countries have done in providing the first citizen of this country with a residence in which he may receive distinguished guests from at home and abroad".
Briefly, the Act provided that: (a) the Minister of Public Works would furnish, maintain heat and keep the building in repair: (b) the Federal District Commission would maintain the land and improve it as required; (c) the Governor in Council could appoint a steward or housekeeper and other employees deemed necessary for the management of the residence, and fix their rate of remuneration and conditions of employment; (d) the steward or housekeeper could from time to time engage casual employees to assist the regular staff; (e) the Prime Minister's chauffeur could be provided with lodging without charge; (f) moneys appropriated by Parliament for the operation of the residence could be used for the payment of the remuneration of the staff, for the purchase of food and other supplies required for the serving of food, for cleaning, laundering, and the ordinary maintenance of a residence and for defraying other costs of official hospitality provided by the Prime Minister; (g) the Prime Minister would pay to the Receiver General of Canada $5,000 yearly for food and lodging for himself and his family. The last provision was included at the personal insistence of the then Prime Minister, the Rt. Hon. Louis Stephen St. Laurent. Nine years after, on June 16, 1959, the Act was amended in order to bring within its scope the Harrington Lake (Lac Mousseau) Residence. Again as a

August 9, 1977
Order Paper Questions
result of a consensus among all parties the Bill went through all stages in one day. In his opening remarks, its sponsor, the Hon. Howard C. Green, Minister of Public Works, referred to a question which Mr. H. W. Herridge of the CCF had asked a few weeks earlier in the following terms: ".. . In view of the general concern that the historic and beautiful Harrington Lake residence and property be preserved and used to the best advantage, will the government recognize this concern and interest by the introduction of legislation that will establish this property as an official government country residence for use by the Prime Minister, his distinguished guests and other appropriate persons?".
After mentioning that he had replied that legislation could be introduced during the current session "should it be the wish generally of hon. members that such a course be followed", Mr. Green went on to say that this proviso had been added ". . . because legislation of this kind is not the type that any government wishes to introduce, and in particular that no prime minister wishes to have introduced, unless members are agreed that such steps should be taken. I remember the reaction of Right Hon. Mr. St. Laurent when the Prime Minister's Residence Act was introduced originally, and it was just the same as the reaction of the present Prime Minister to this proposed amendment. These men, in a position of great responsibility, think of themselves last. If it were not the wish of the house generally to have the amendment which 1 am moving today passed, the government would not, of course, proceed with the measure. May I hasten to add that the other members of the cabinet-and 1 am sure the members of the last cabinet-feel very keenly that this measure is appropriate and, as a matter of fact, is badly needed in order to help ease the burdens of whoever may happen to be the prime minister of this nation."
It will be recalled that nine years earlier, in 1950, a group of citizens representing all parties and residents in all of the provinces had purchased a property called Stornoway located in the village of Rockcliffe Park as an official residence for the Leader of the Official Opposition as they felt that the holder of that office should be provided with a residence consistent with the meaning and dignity of his position. These citizens, and others who were added over the years, maintained the property until 1971 when the government introduced a Bill entitled an "Act to amend the Prime Minister's Residence Act", which provided among others for the transfer of Stornoway to the government at no cost and its maintenance in the future out of public funds as an official residence for the Leader of the Official Opposition. As stated by the sponsor of the Bill, the Hon. Allan J. MacEachen, President of the Privy Council, the trustees, whose Chairman was the Hon. Grattan O'Leary, having carried the cost and care of the administration of the property for 20 years had concluded that its ownership and administration should justly pass into the hands of the Government and, as Senator O'Leary had put it, "become a part of the parliamentary structure". The Bill also proposed to give statutory recognition to the occupation on a rent-free basis by the Speaker of the House of Commons of the

building and associated grounds known as The Farm and located at Kingsmere, Quebec. Finally, in keeping with the recommendations of the Advisory Committee on Parliamentary Salaries and Expenses (Beaupre Report) it provided that neither the Prime Minister nor the Leader of the Official Opposition should be required to pay rent for publicly owned residences provided for their official use. There was however a stipulation that the financial outlay of $5,000 then payable by the Prime Minister on his residence would continue at that rate until the day after the following general election. Again, there was a large degree of support in the House for the Bill. Referring to the provisions regarding Stornoway, the spokesman for the Official Opposition noted that it underlined "the importance of the man who is the number one critic of those in power, and the number one contender for succession when the people's will is expressed in another way" and that "of all the variations of the democratic parliamentary system, the one whereby the Leader of the Opposition is made, in fact, an official part of the system is a fine move". As to the changes involving the Prime Minister's residence his comments were that they were long overdue. The spokesman for the New Democratic Party concurred in this view that the Prime Minister should not be asked to contribute $5,000 annually recalling that it had originally been included at the personal insistence of Mr. St. Laurent: ". . .A case can certainly be made for our not requiring that, for if we are going to provide the Prime Minister with a residence in which he can live and in which he must be one of the nation's hosts, it does seem proper that we take care of the cost of it.. ." ". . . However, I am interested in the fact that the proposal to discontinue the requirement that this $5,000 a year be paid by the Prime Minister does not come into effect until the end of this parliament. It comes into effect on the day of the general election following dissolution of the 28th Parliament. No one knows who will be the occupant of that house at that point, but at any rate here is a clear case of deciding that a certain monetary benefit to one of the members of this House shall not accrue to him until after the next election".
The Bill received Royal Assent on June 10, 1971. During the 26 years that have elapsed since the passage of the original legislation, the House, through the normal process of scrutiny and approval of estimates and asking of oral and written questions, has carefully watched the spending of public expenditures for official residences and did not hesitate to question some of them whenever it deemed it necessary. A study of the Official Report of the House of Commons Debates for that period, which extends over a quarter of a century, shows on the other hand that successive governments have not hesitated to provide information in reply to inquiries from Members. See for instance, among others, replies to questions No. 804, 2,598 and 2,601 of the first session of the 29th Parliament and No. 45, 86, 87, 88, and 89 of the second session; and No. 1,351, 1,666, 1,667, 1,668, 1,669, 2,307, 2,523, 2,790, 2,793, 2,794, 3,236, 3,471 and 5,203 of the first session, 30th Parliament. subtopic: QUESTIONS ON THE ORDER PAPER
subsubtopic: FEDERAL MONETARY POLICIES IN QUEBEC AND THE ATLANTIC PROVINCES
speechtext:
Is the government taking any new initiatives to ease the government's restrictive monetary policies in Quebec and the Atlantic Provinces and, if necessary, to reverse them in slow growth areas in Eastern Canada where tight money has an instant, lasting and disastrous effect?
Mr. Bob Kaplan (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of
Finance): The government does not have a restrictive monetary policy at the present time. Monetary policy is directed at achieving moderate growth consistent with continued progress in reducing the rate of inflation. As the rate of inflation has moderated, it has become possible to lower the bank rate, on four separate occasions since last November, to 7V) per cent where it now stands. These downward adjustments to the bank rate were necessary to push the growth of the money supply up towards the 8 to 12 per cent target range specified by the Governor of the Bank of Canada. In times of restrictive monetary policy, when money for loans is scarce, the Governor of the Bank of Canada has used moral suasion to encourage the chartered banks to have a special regard for the credit needs of the slower growth areas of the country. Nevertheless,
August 9, 1977

it is difficult to differentiate the stance of monetary policy in Quebec and the Atlantic Provinces from that in the rest of Canada. The Bank of Canada must operate in capital markets that are national in scope. If the Bank were to inject funds into Quebec and the Atlantic Provinces to lower interest rates in these regions, private funds would flow out of these regions seeking the higher interest rates in the rest of Canada. The outflow would continue until interest rates were comparable across Canada. Thus, the initial stimulus would be spread throughout the country and not retained in Quebec and the Atlantic Provinces where it was initially injected. Fiscal policy can be regionally differentiated much more satisfactorily than monetary policy. It has long been the practice of the government to distribute a significant portion of government expenditure on a basis which is favourable to higher than average unemployment areas. Some current examples of the government's use of regional differentiation of fiscal policy appear in our treatment of the investment tax credit and direct job creation in the March 31 Budget. The investment tax credit has been increased from 5 per cent to 10 per cent in the Atlantic Provinces, the Gaspe area and the Magdalen Islands; and to I'h per cent in areas designated under the Regional Development Incentives Act in Saskatchewan, Manitoba, Northern Ontario and Quebec (other than the Gaspe Region). Of the $1.2 billion the government plans to spend on manpower programs in 1977-78, $458 million is committed to the direct employment strategy. As was stated in the last Budget, this strategy, which includes the Canada Works, Young Canada Works, and Local Initiatives Programs among others, is designed to have a greater impact in the higher unemployment areas of Canada. In addition to these two specific initiatives must be added the ongoing activities of the Departments of Regional Economic Expansion and of Industry, Trade and Commerce aimed toward improving the economic performance of regions experiencing comparatively high unemployment.

As the hon. member will be aware, absolute privilege attaches to such correspondence when production is sought in legal proceedings. This is so by reason of subsection 41(2) of the Federal Court Act. He said: Mr. Speaker, it gives me no great pleasure to introduce this bill today. To ask parliament to approve a bill to end a legal strike is something which this government and which I, as Minister of Labour, do not welcome. Collective bargaining is part of our democratic way of life. It is the best system that has been devised for the voluntary regulation of the demands of employers and workers. It is not a perfect system, but in most situations it works, and it works well. Under collective bargaining, employers can anticipate with great certainty their labour costs and they can anticipate prolonged periods of labour peace. On the other hand, organized workers have been able to establish a fair return for their labour and they have improved their working conditions, largely as a result of their efforts at the bargaining table. Unorganized workers, to a considerable extent, have received improved wages and conditions that are influenced by improvements negotiated in the organized sector.
There has been considerable public comment of late about the incidence of strikes in this country. Canada's reputation in this regard has lately been greatly distorted, but the situation recently has improved greatly: strikes and lock-outs have not been resorted to frequently. Canada's record is not a record of numerous strikes and lock-outs, but of strikes and lock-outs which continue for a long period. Losses due to strikes and lock-outs in Canada this year are showing a sharp improvement over last year and recent years. I believe the anti-inflation program can be given much of the credit for this improvement.

For the first four months of this year, the loss in man-days was only 0.18 for every 10,000 days worked. In federal industries and in the federal public service man-day losses have been insignificant.
This government has recognized the importance of improving labour relations in this country. Last October, in the Speech from the Throne, improved labour relations was one of the three or four matters which we said deserved priority attention of parliament. The others included national unity and human rights. In the debate on the Speech from the Throne I summarized a 14-point program for improving our labour relations system. Since that time I have met with representatives of labour and industry to enlist their co-operation in putting some of these programs into effect. As the basis of many of these programs is our determination to find a better way to diminish the adversarial approach by employers and trade unions at the bargaining table and create a better environment in which collective bargaining can occur. This can be done if we move away from the confrontation that characterizes so many of our negotiations. We also want to improve working conditions, including health and safety, for all Canadian workers.
Mr. Speaker, in the situation which has caused you to call all members back to the House we have a strike by the Canadian Air Traffic Controllers Association against the government. CATCA called this strike because it saw no other way to resolve its differences with the government negotiators at the bargaining table.
We have to ask ourselves who is bearing the brunt of this action. We have to recognize the right to strike. With ad hoc legislation of this kind it is always a value judgment of any government of the day to weigh whether it should permit a strike to continue for a prolonged period of time or whether, in the circumstances, the interests of parties not party to the negotiations and not at the bargaining table should assume paramountcy in terms of responsibility of the government and parliament of the day. We believe that in terms of the judgment we are exercising, the interests of those not at the table are paramount and we should consider the interests of those Canadians injuriously affected by a prolongation of this strike.
We know there are many innocent third parties to this dispute. It falls on members of the travelling public who are caught by surprise and who will have great difficulty in

changing their vacations and completing their travel plans while this strike continues. One estimate shows that 35,000 to 40,000 Canadians are travelling by air each day at this time of the year. This is a serious inconvenience when you consider not only these Canadians but the tens of thousands of others they were intending to meet at the end of their flight.
Second, the burden falls on others who are not at the bargaining table. It falls on the airlines, which last year experienced difficult business conditions and have been operating at a loss. Some estimates show the airlines could lose as much as $5 million to $6 million a day while the strike continues. This situation could have serious repercussions for all air carriers. Other airline employees are also affected. The ground crews which service the aircraft, the baggage handlers, and sales and reservation clerks, the airline crews-these workers are all covered by collective agreements and they are affected.
It is hard to think of a business or a town or city in Canada which is not affected by this work stoppage. Every hour of every day that this strike continues is causing severe inconvenience to the travelling public and interrupting business and industry with their hundreds and thousands of employees which depend on the delivery of goods by air.
It is not the purpose of this legislation to take away the right to strike from CATCA. But it is the purpose of this bill to end this strike as soon as possible. CATCA was given the right to strike from the day it was certified as an employee association more than ten years ago under the Public Service Staff Relations Acts. The government did not pre-empt the right to strike. This bill does not take away that right; rather, it is a value judgment for the reasons I have outlined. As one of the unions in the public service, CATCA has enjoyed the right to strike since 1967. But it must use the right wisely and responsibly. Like few other unions in the public sector or the private sector, it holds a juggernaut position in its industry. It is in a position to impose sanctions of the most severe kind on the whole country. When the air traffic controllers served notice last week that they would institute a series of rotating strikes, and later a total strike, they knew they were exerting a monopoly power which could bring a vital national industry to its knees.
I might very briefly refer to the history of this dispute. The essence of the dispute is the difference between the union and the employer over the money clause. The parties were assisted in their attempts to reach a settlement by a three-man conciliation board, one nominated by the union, one by the employer, and a chairman agreed on by the parties. All three members of the conciliation board concurred in recommending an 8 per cent increase in total compensation. This unanimous recommendation was made after giving due consideration to AIB guidelines.
It has been an accepted procedure in our attempts to reach a settlement in a dispute to go along with a conciliation board report. There is added justification when the board report on the major item at issue is unanimous, as this one in the air traffic controllers' dispute was. Hon. members will recall that
August 9, 1977

we proceeded to a settlement on the basis of Commissioner Perry's report in the west coast grain industry dispute, and on the basis of the report of Judge Gold, acting as a commissioner in the St. Lawrence River longshoring dispute.
Two major obstacles to a settlement relate to rates of pay before conversion and rates of pay resulting from conversion with respect to reclassification of jobs. The content of the revised classification standard has been essentially agreed to, although there is disagreement as to the slotting of some jobs within the new standard.
Dealing with the rates of pay before conversion, it is clear from the record that what Treasury Board negotiators agreed to was the maximum permissible level under the guidelines in terms of 8 per cent total compensation. On the rates of pay applicable after conversion, that is, the cost of conversion, CATCA says the cost is to be excluded from the application of the AIB guidelines. The employer says it must be included in the guidelines allowable. This is consistent with AIB guidelines. In essence, CATCA demanded an increase of more than 12.6 per cent, when the guidelines would allow a maximum of 8 per cent.
If the employer were to capitulate to the CATCA demand in the face of a strike threat, or now an existing strike, the government would be condoning a settlement in excess of the AIB guidelines. Such a solution is clearly unacceptable. The government could then be accused, with justification, of asking for restraint from business and labour in the private sector and not practising restraint in negotiations with its own employees.
The government could allow the strike, now that it has been called, to run its course. That is one alternative. This might be seen by some as being compatible with free collective bargaining. But should the strike last for a considerable period, or even for a few more days, the public would be held for ransom and the airlines subjected to punishing damage. The government, then, has introduced this bill to end a dispute which can only, unfortunately, go from bad to worse, by requiring the air traffic controllers to return to work immediately.
It is with great reluctance that we have called upon Your Honour to bring back the House to deal with this emergency bill, but it is the view of the government that it is in the national interest that parliament should give this measure its unanimous approval.

It is all very well for hon. members and for people in the media and in other places to decide that because a strike has now occurred, all the blame lies with the union. I do not even think the Minister of Labour (Mr. Munro) would go that far. But that suggestion lies under the surface in this chamber and in other places. The fact is, the blame does not all lie with the union.
For many years the government has constantly talked about the right to strike, yet has consistently refused to act in accordance with our insistence that some mechanism be provided to do two things-to deal with those areas which involve essential services and where the government knows it will bring in legislation to end a strike in any event, and other cases where a strike might not begin as an "essential service" strike but the ultimate effect of which upon the economy might be such as to justify its conclusion, in the public interest.
The Minister of Labour says, "Don't take away the right to strike; don't have compulsory arbitration", and so on. There is nothing more compulsory than that which is being done here today. The Minister of Labour gave us all the reasons why this lawful strike should not be taking place. Then he says, "This does not mean we do not think the right to strike should exist in this particular area". He cannot have it both ways. The Minister of Labour is trying to say, "Don't, whatever you do, think we would restrain the right to strike under any circumstances at all except those circumstances under which we think it should not be exercised".
If we are to find a way by which in certain areas the country is not, to quote the minister's words, to be held up to ransom, we must find a way to deal with situations such as this. If Your Honour would read the speeches I have made on various occasions on behalf of my party when strikes have been settled by legislation, you would find I have repeatedly urged the government to devise a mechanism which would solve this difficulty. What happened to the Woods report? The minister will no doubt say that the Woods report was handed down a long time ago. It certainly was. But it did deal with this problem, and whatever the defects in its recommendations may have been, it certainly recognized the nature of the difficulty we face.
The minister began by seeking the general sympathy of the nation by describing the inconvenience, familiar to everyone, which a lot of people are suffering. Then he tried to persuade us, by strange logic, that it did not matter because the collective bargaining system was working in cases of this kind. It is too laughable for words. Nothing will be done, Mr. COMMONS DEBATES

Speaker, until the Minister of Labour and others on the government side admit that in certain cases the right to strike, though it may be de jure, is not de facto. Hon. members opposite know this to be a true statement of the position. It was said during the railway strike some years ago by the negotiators for the railway unions that the right to strike was a myth, that it existed only provided it was not used or was ineffective.
What has happened in this case? Under the Public Service Staff Relations Act, CATCA elected to take the conciliation strike route which was laid out by the government in legislation years ago. What has the Minister of Transport done? He has said to CATCA, "I intend to make up my mind as to what you should get, and if you don't agree with me I shall legislate what 1 think you should get and legislate you back to work if you go on strike". Where is the arbitrator in all this, the other side of the public service staff relations procedure? Mr. Speaker, if a union does not wish to take the strike route, it chooses the arbitration route and accepts binding arbitration.
What the government has done is this: it set up legislation and told the union it could take its choice. The strike route was chosen. Then the government told them it was not acceptable and declined even to substitute an arbitrator. The arbitrator is the Minister of Transport, with his notion of what the settlement ought to be. I ask you, Mr. Speaker, what would you do if this were not a public service union? What would you do if it were a union which came under the federal government, under the Canada Labour Code, and got into difficulties. Suppose it were the CNR or a public owned railway such as the CNR which came to parliament and said, "Our fellows will not settle on anything reasonable. We have our own views as to what the settlement should be, and we want the House of Commons to legislate them back to work on terms agreeable to us". Would that be fair? Would this House accept such a proposal? No. Yet this is what has happened today.
We agree that the strike should not have taken place, but we say a good deal of the blame for it lies right over there in the seat of the Minister of Transport.

I am not suggesting that everything about labour relations in Europe is necessarily better or applicable in this country. I would be the last person to suggest-and the Minister of Labour is aware of this-that you can take situations which happen in other countries and transplant them into our milieu. But in a number of countries, air traffic controllers are operating basically within the same technical range of problems, with the same basic sophistication of equipment and the same responsibility. However, their record of continuance of service is amazingly better than in this country. I am referring to nations such as the United States, Great Britain, West Germany, France, Sweden, Holland, Belgium and others.
Is it beyond the measure of this House to suggest we find out why it works elsewhere, and not here? Is it beyond the measure of this House to put aside the rhetoric of the right to strike and decide to figure out proper settlements, fair settlements, settlements which will confirm an even number of highly qualified people to serve the public, without always getting into a confrontation and strike action? Yes, a 63 per cent improvement in terms of reduced strikes. Obviously, the minister did not make any direct connection with the controls program, with the fact that it did not make much sense for workers to go on strike, if they contravened the law of Canada. Being law-abiding citizens, most workers do not do that sort of thing. I would have thought there was some connection between that improvement and the controls program, which some people have, not inappropriately, described as fascism with a human face. If the minister is really concerned about the record of labour in Canada this year, he would have been more concerned with another statistic which the government has produced, to the effect that some two billion man-hours have been lost because of unemployment. That is the record of the government so far in 1977.
Let me come to the point about mendacity. The minister got to his feet and said that it moved him to tears almost to bring in such legislation, because workers in this great, free society do have the right to strike. I do agree that at some point, even when there is a right to strike, a government which is responsible has to move in and say that in the public good this right has to be sacrificed. 1 do not think there is a contradiction
there. In a free society you often have conflicts in rights, liberties and obligations and you have to choose. But it is a phony argument to give the right to strike to a group of workers and then to tell them, before they even act upon the right to strike, that the government will bring in legislation. That, to me, is hypocritical. You cannot have that argument. I agree with the Conservative party on this: logically, you cannot have it both ways. If you give the right to strike to a particular sector, then the workers must exercise that right, if it is to mean anything at all. That is my first point.
More significantly, Mr. Speaker, the minister said that a conciliation board report was made. He said that the conciliation board made a unanimous recommendation which the government was acting on. Implicitly, the minister said, "Therefore, how can any reasonable person not accept this conciliation board report presented by representatives of labour as well as 'the bad guys'"? I wondered what the minister was talking about, so I checked. As the minister knows very well, the reclassification issue, which is the essence of this strike, was beyond the terms of reference of the conciliation board. The minister knows full well that when the conciliation board recommended solutions to the government and the union, it said in its report that the reclassification issue was something that the government had to work out with the union.
Did the minister tell the House that the conciliation board had looked at the 8 per cent package and had made a unanimous recommendation? Did he say that they had examined the issue which this strike is all about? He did not tell us that at all. He deliberately tried to leave the impression with the House and with the people of Canada that the union involved was going against a conciliation board report that was unanimous. In that respect I say he misled the House and he was trying to mislead the people of Canada.
I want to come to what I think the strike is all about. I say at the outset that if you look at the half-dozen pieces of back-to-work legislation which have been brought before the House of Commons, you will see that my party has supported more than half of them. We have not taken the position, under all the circumstances, that the right to strike is sacred and can never be sacrificed at all. That is not the case. Sometimes, as I said at the outset, the public interest will require a shift and will require that some rights be traded-off against others. But what we object to, and why we are opposed to this bill-and not only state our opposition, as have the Conservatives, but will vote against it unless there is some change-is that the government produced this strike It was not CATCA. It was not a group of working people in Canada who produced this strike. The government of Canada and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Lang) are responsible.
The reason I reached this conclusion is that there is one point of substance that distinguishes the position of the government from that of the union. The point of substance concerns reclassification. As we all know from public statements made

August 9, 1977

by Treasury Board officials, by ministers, by the Prime Minister (Mr. Trudeau) himself, and from private conversations I have had in the past 24 hours with the ministers and with the Prime Minister, the issue revolves around two different approaches. The government has said that they will not go beyond the 8 per cent. Their analysis of CATCA's proposals, their reading of the ideas presented by the union, was that by including the reclassification proposal of CATCA, the guidelines of the AIB would be broken; therefore, they would not go beyond 8 per cent.
I say that the government can make at least a reasonable case for its interpretation; I agree with that. What the union has said is that if you look at the regulations which flow from the AIB, you can make a good case for saying that in addition to the 8 per cent there is roughly another 4.5 per cent to which the workers are entitled because of the reclassification that has been accepted by the government.
I want to get back to the cause of the strike. For once, I share the Prime Minister's view of the media. I say to those ladies and gentleman in the press gallery, "You have some obligation for once to convey the honest and accurate position of a group of workers in Canada to the people of Canada, so that they will understand that this government is responsible for the strike".

The Prime Minister is saying that the government would accept the 12 per cent if the AIB so ruled. I ask, why were they so hypocritical in their approach, or at least not serious in their bargaining with the CATCA people, when they said, "Submit the two approaches to AIB"? What the government
Air Traffic Controllers
is saying to the union is that the AIB should become the arbitration board, which it is not. It is a misuse of the AIB to follow that approach.
Second, from the union's point of view they were saying to the workers in Canada, "Why don't you submit this bargaining item to the AIB and hope that they will choose the richer package?" They are saying that if the two are submitted, the AIB may come down and choose the richer. Surely at this point in our history, when Canadians are so concerned about inflation and unemployment, it was reasonable for the union to say that it did not make sense for them to submit a richer and a poorer package because, quite plausibly, it is more likely the AIB would accept the poorer package. So the union, quite correctly, rejected this approach. They said, "Let us not, because the AIB is not an arbitration board, have them solve the dispute between us and the government; and let us not, on behalf of our members, take the chance that they will opt for the poorer package when we think we are entitled to the richer package".
I think that is a responsible approach. But beyond that-this is the message I want to give, through you, Mr. Speaker, to the people of Canada-this union was not insisting that the government accept the richer package. All the union said was, "If you submit that particular package to the AIB, we will accept their decision." I repeat that Treasury Board had indicated they would accept the richer package if the AIB ruled on it. If that had been done, there would have been no strike, parliament would not be sitting now, and thousands of Canadians from coast to coast who have been inconvenienced would not have suffered the consequences of the strike.
As recently as yesterday I consulted the union to clarify this approach in order to make sure that that is what they had in mind. I read the reports during the weekend. They spoke to our party and to other parties in the House of Commons. It became clear that that was the issue. Following that, I spoke with the Prime Minister twice and said to him, "The union has said that the country would be back to normal within six hours, its members back to work, and the planes could be flying if you modify your approach. You said the richer package is acceptable if the AIB rules on it. Why don't you submit it to the AIB and let them decide?" If the government had done that, CATCA says that planes would have been flying within six hours. But the government said no because, I suspect, a guy named Otto Lang locked them, again, into a stupid position, an arbitrary position.

subtopic: AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT
subsubtopic: AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS-MEASURE TO END STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, once again the members of the House of Commons have been recalled to pass back-to-work legislation for hundreds of workers who have seen fit to strike as a result of a misunderstanding with the authorities of air transport services. It is not the first time that such a thing has happened. A few years ago, we were recalled in similar circumstances in connection with the CN employees and longshoremen. It should be normal as a result of such cases for the government to pass more flexible legislation to avoid such conflicts. The labour legislation must be designed to maintain some balance between the just demands of workers and the requirement of the common good.
In public services, the economic powers proceeding from the right to strike should be replaced by a proper mechanism to adjust wages according to the cost of living index.
I understand that it becomes rather difficult in a control period but we are now at least approaching a decontrol period. After controlling, they are now trying to decontrol. Obviously,
August 9, 1977

under such circumstances, it becomes more difficult to adjust the wages of a team of air services employees.
We should stop thinking in terms of compulsory contributions or conciliation and consider instead a fairer distribution of the enterprise's profits and the workers' wages. With all the inquiry commissions that have been created, with all the civil servants getting various wages, and some of them are quite high, with all those people conducting on-going studies on the ways to improve the employees' working conditions in Canada, it seems to me that it should be possible to find a just solution. Obviously, this solution will not be found without efforts, but the present situation teaches us that we must take the appropriate means if we really want to avoid anarchy.
There are important factors to be considered when establishing an employee's working conditions. We must not forget that the employee is a human being, not a machine, and that he is looking for security and stability. In general terms, he wants his working place to be well organized and well managed. It is normal that he should be treated with justice. The employee also wants to be informed on his employer's business situation so as to know he may get a fair income. Those are basic realities. In no circumstances should an employee endanger his life to earn a living. Workers are the first naturally entitled to know clearly and fully their specific working conditions. They should also have the possibility to refuse, without any salary loss, to do a work they consider dangerous for their health and security till a decision is made by an authorized committee.
Workers' health and security must be fully secured, regardless of any ideology which in any case could not disturb with impunity the scientific data more and more verifiable by both parties. It is important to emphasize that man, not profit, should be the central point of any social project if we want to have the privilege of being part of the establishment of the new economic order which is more and more referred to by the most thoughtful people.
Basically this implies a new moral order or a new scale of values. Workers, through their organizations are and remain the main factors of change as far as their whole collective development and progress are concerned. All workers should understand that unionism is not an end in itself but a means of ensuring the promotion and the progress of workers in general. Considering that this means is limited they must seek and accept the methods which can help them meet the objectives of unionism.
In this age of automation, the worker is a man or a woman who is concerned about the future and anxious to take full advantage of technological progress. The worker's concern stems from the fact that he is aware that our society is not organized to distribute fairly this new wealth produced by science, technology and machine with a minimum of human participation. The worker lives in a society which is unable to adapt itself properly to progress.
On July 5, 1972, during a debate on the longshoremen's strike, 1 told the House that we were living in a system so unbalanced that citizens have concluded that certain grievances can be settled only by striking. However, we must
Air Traffic Controllers
logically recognize that everything that has been accomplished in the world is the result of work. No one can deny this. How is it that thousands of workers decide that their problems can be solved by a work stoppage? A strike is simply illogical. It is a phenomenon related to various generalized illnesses and which becomes a hypothetical means of pressure since the decision to strike must be submitted to a vote and since decisions are often made by only a percentage of the workers involved.
In general, strikes are aimed against those who pay instead of those who deprive. I am surprised to see that in the many strikes that occur in Canada, the workers have a tendency to strike against those who pay them instead of organizing a true general strike, as they should, against the financial system which is depriving everyone. This would be somewhat more logical in my opinion.
You need to have very little imagination or to refuse to see the disastrous results of a financial system divorced from current economic realities not to conclude that strikes are most often the result of demands for salary readjustment or increases. Why? It is very easy to find an answer. Successive wage increases cannot catch up with the increase in the cost of living, and metaphorically speaking, we could say that wages go up by the stairs while consumer prices go up by the elevator.
The evolution of automation, which should be beneficial, has become the nightmare of thousands of workers in the present system.
The various employee associations seem to want the industry or the employer to absorb all the expenses that result from mechanized installation, as well as wage readjustments and all the demands brought about by a sick financial system.
I have often underlined the delays caused by ever more strikes and I added that sometimes it was a necessary evil which we should avoid spreading.
One of the well known leader of the American labour movement, Mr. George Meany, once pointed out that in unduly protracted conflicts employees bear a financial burden disproportionate to the advantages they could gain from a confrontation and it is actually a fact.
Given the present situation and the lack of provisions in a legislation which is not adopted to the circumstances, we wonder if some solution other than a settlement imposed by Parliament could not be found under the present circumstances.
Unfortunately, we come to the conclusion that the answer is no. There is no alternative to settling that problem other than ordering a return to work through government legislation. It is to be hoped that this legislation will be adopted and that strikers will realize their responsibilities.
The strikers should go back to work without waiting for the adoption of lengthy procedures which do not solve the problems. We already have too many examples of settlements against the workers. We need but mention the case of the employees of G. Lapalme Inc. working for the Post Office

August 9, 1977
Air Traffic Controllers
department. We have suggested repeatedly, and we are not the only ones to have done so, many authorities in the field of labour have as well, the possibility of setting up labour tribunals, real ones. Of the proposals we made in this House, let me quote this one, section 3 which reads as follows:
(3) to make an adequate evaluation of the viability of the undertaking or service, taking into consideration the risks, the cash reserves required to ensure its operations, tax deductions and such formalities as result from tax regulations;
Many things must be taken into account.
A labour court made up of government, business and workers' representatives to consider regularly questions of relations between workers and management, which would not wait six months after the expiration of contracts to begin negotiations. At the time of contract renewal, on-going negotiations should take place and every interested party should be made aware of the proposals, because worthy investigations would have been made by representatives of all parties concerned. At that time, I have good reason to believe that the workers, who are as intelligent as anybody else of any other class of people, would understand that, due to circumstances, this offer would be acceptable. I am wondering whether those responsible for air services did not hesitate too much. I have here an article written by Michel Roy of Le Devoir who is certainly aware of a number of things, because he writes, and 1 quote:
CATCA proposed to the government to conclude the agreement and submit the whole thing to the Anti-Inflation Board, feeling that it would have to make the distinction in its analyses between a wage increase benefiting all controllers and a wage increase resulting from a reclassification. The union representatives are even prepared to give the undertaking and abide by the decision of the board when it is made.
I believe this unfortunate conflict could have been avoided.
The government, for its part, refused to refer a wage settlement to the board-
But why did we set up that famous board? For a year and a half we discussed in committee the possibility of setting up a board. It seems to me to be inoperative at this time.
And that is why all commercial aviation in this country has been paralyzed for the past 48 hours, with daily losses to air carriers being estimated at more than $5 million without counting opportunities lost by industries that depend on air transport or the hard-to-assess inconveniences of all kinds that thousands of users must undergo.
I think that if there had been a little more goodwill from those in charge that conflict could have been avoided.
I conclude by mentioning the suggestion we made and we continue to make because we have excellent reason to believe it could be right-the formation of a labour court with the responsibilities and the power to decide something. At that time, as I say, I have excellent reason to believe that we would avoid conflicts such as the one we are now faced with.
However, we are not short of examples on which the government could meditate. I have here an article from the newspaper Le Droit of August 31, 1973, under the following heading, and 1 quote:
Strikers Storm Parliament.
It seems to me that this should be reason enough for government members to make up their minds and put forward an adequate labour legislation that would meet the needs of
[Mr. Dionne (Kamouraska).l
the majority of the people. I know full well it is easier to criticize than to govern. But we are really looking for something in the government's proposals that would give a way out. If we had the labour court that would be needed in various regions, with representatives from all interested parties, it would investigate and suggest practical solutions to the parties before a labour agreement had come to an end, and this should be a settlement. I submit the government should do this.

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert K. Andras (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT
subsubtopic: AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS-MEASURE TO END STRIKE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my comments I want to outline the four major unresolved areas, areas outstanding when negotiations broke off, in order that the government's position will be known and understood. The first concerns money. In changing the system by which air traffic controllers' jobs are classified, there are, of course, assumed automatic increases in pay. It is the government's position that the total compensation received as a result of job reclassification, as well as the negotiated increase in the basic negotiations, is subject to the maximum allowable compensation increase, as set out in the AIB arithmetic guidelines, of 8 per cent. CATCA, on the other hand, is demanding that pay increases which come as a result of the reclassification should be treated separately from those which are negotiated under the collective agreement. Adoption of their version would have meant, in the first year alone, an additional 4.6 per cent compensation increase beyond the arithmetic 8 per cent guidelines.
The government proposed a conversion cost of less than one-half of 1 per cent which, of course, was within the over-all guideline limit of 8 per cent. CATCA, however, rejected that.
I shall return to the point of classification pay in a few minutes. As the leader of the NDP indicated, when you boil it down, that is one of the basic issues in this matter.
The second issue is vacations. CATCA wanted to provide its members with five weeks vacation after 20 years of service. At present, only CATCA and one other union have a contract which provides five weeks vacation after 25 years of service. All other federal public service collective agreements provide for five weeks vacation after 27 years of service or more. The third issue deals with management rights. CATCA is demanding at present that a minimum of two controllers be on duty at all airports at certain times. CATCA also wanted a change of work hours for non-operating controllers. To accede to these two latter demands would increase the number of controllers over-all and increase the cost of operations. More important, it is management's view and management's right to say that it is not necessary from an operational standpoint.
The fourth issue is classification. CATCA was demanding that some 100 jobs be put in a higher classification than the job responsibilities merit.

speechtext:
There was also the pension issue, was there not?
August 9, 1977

subtopic: AIR TRAFFIC CONTROL SERVICES CONTINUATION ACT
subsubtopic: AIR TRAFFIC CONTROLLERS-MEASURE TO END STRIKE
speechtext:
I am trying to deal with the major outstanding ones, not one where there is a possibility of resolution.
CATCA also wanted a change of work hours for nonoperating controllers. Of course, that-as I have already indicated-would be an additional cost. Realistically-this was pointed out by a previous speaker-the most significant and controversial of these issues is the total increase in compensation payable under the anti-inflation guidelines.
The government is absolutely convinced that 8 per cent is the absolute maximum increase allowable under the AntiInflation Act, and that should include the basic increase and the conversion cost of reclassification for CATCA. The government is not prepared deliberately to sign an agreement which includes and supports or implies support for an increase larger than permissible under the Anti-Inflation Act and its regulations, leaving the onus on the AIB to roll back that excess. The anti-inflation guidelines do provide several conditions under which compensation increases for a group may be exempt from the maximum arithmetic increase permitted under the guidelines, the six plus two in this particular case. The most important of those conditions for exemptions are as follows: first, the historical relationship with another group; second, where there has been persistent and serious recruiting difficulties, as was the case with the prison guards; third, permission to achieve a minimum wage of $3.75 an hour, or $600 per year, whichever is the highest. The fourth would deal with a commitment prior to October 14, 1975, to provide compensation increases to a group.
Obviously, none of the first three conditions apply in the current air traffic controllers' dispute. Nor does the fourth- that is, prior commitment-although 1 think in some peoples minds they considered that possibility. The fourth condition, that of prior commitment, was designed to apply to collective agreements signed before October 14, 1975, which provided increases in the period following that date. Also, it was designed to apply to commitments made, but where contracts had not been formally signed to increase a group's compensation after October 14, 1975.
The Anti-Inflation Board has made it absolutely clear in its regulations and in its pattern of settlements and its decisions that to qualify as an allowable exemption such priority cannot be a simple expression of intent to increase compensation. That commitment must be thoroughly identifiable and capable of quantification in terms of cost.
There is a pattern to this that is absolutely clear. When it is boiled down, as the leader of the NDP has said, the major issue between the Canadian Air Traffic Control Association, Treasury Board and the government is the status of the cost of converting air traffic controllers to the new classification plan. Both time and the terms of reference of the work on that new classification plan disqualified such costs from exemption under the anti-inflation guidelines.
It is very important that I set before hon. members the sequence of events relating to the work of the new classifica-
Air Traffic Controllers
tion plan for the air traffic control group. In early 1975, the Ministry of Transport decided to undertake an internal study of the air traffic control classification standard. In June, 1975, CATCA responded positively to an invitation to take part in that project. The terms of reference of that study were to examine the classification standard for the group, with the objective of determining its strengths and its weaknesses. Following that first phase, a second study was foreseen to look at the causes of problems, to design alternatives and to recommend specific courses of action.
On October 1, 1975, the Ministry of Transport sent a copy of the phase one report to the president of CATCA. In the letter which accompanied this report, the ministry indicated that it was studying the report to determine what steps should be taken to remedy some of the problems. It indicated that "one possibility"-I repeat, "one possibility"-under active consideration could be a full-scale revision to the classification standard. The letter indicated that it would seek CATCA's participation in a second phase of the study. Clearly, this report does not indicate any particular course of action. On January 13, 1976, the ministry wrote to the president of CATCA informing him that the conduct of the second phase of the internal study had been approved, and confirmed earlier participation of an executive member of CATCA. That is after the AIB regulations came into effect.
The date, terms of reference and directions are particularly significant in terms of the current disagreement. The terms of reference were to develop a new classification standard for the air traffic control occupational group which would to the greatest extent possible satisfy the following requirements: resolve the problem issues, provide a basis for ensuring equitable salary, and be acceptable to the employer. The committee was also to re-examine the point-rating method of re-evaluation. I want to stress that this was an internal study, because the leader of the NDP, quite rightly, focused on this area of possible prior commitment in some of his comments. When a final proposal was developed, it was to be subject to approval by Treasury Board which, of course, is responsible under the Financial Administration Act.
Consequently, in terms of the Anti-Inflation Board compensation bulletin I, and that board's ruling on what constitutes a commitment made prior to October 14, 1975, Treasury Board is convinced that nothing in the actions taken prior to October 14, 1975, constitutes a prior commitment that would exempt the cost of introducing a new classification plan from the application of the anti-inflation guidelines.
Finally, Mr. Speaker, in June, 1976, CATCA signed its first collective agreement after the anti-inflation program was in effect. There was no demand for a new classification plan when they signed that agreement, and no claim for exemption of resultant costs from anti-inflation guidelines. CATCA clearly does not have a case of prior commitment in terms of a classification program. If they had had a belief in that prior commitment, they certainly would not have turned down the government's offer to include CATCA's position in a signed agreement to be sent to the AIB. With the permission of the

August 9, 1977
Air Traffic Controllers
House, I am quite prepared to table the letters to support the government's contention in that argument. I am prepared to table the two letters referred to, as well as the terms of reference of phase two of the study. I am in the hands of hon. members.
I am satisfied that a case has been established that in the most crucial aspect of this dispute, that is, the classification area, there was no prior commitment. Therefore, there is no justification to include it within the exemptions to the guidelines, which would have been the only alternative the government would have supported.
